# Shepherd of Hermas Chapter 18 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Translator:** SOPHIA | **Source:** Codex Sinaiticus (ch 1-31) / P.Mich. 130 (ch 32+), Shepherd of Hermas 18 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-EC/SHE_018_page_001.jpg

---

## Vision 3, Chapter 10

**1** She showed me a great multitude approaching from afar, and in their midst a man of extraordinary height — taller than the tower itself — with the bearing of a great estate-owner, a magnificent crown on his head, clothed in gleaming white garments. **2** He wore white boots on his feet; in his right hand was a sickle, in his left a shepherd's crook. He came and took his position before the tower. **3** He directed that the stones be brought and fitted into the building. Six young men who were building, along with four others on his right, received the stones and continued the work. **4** He then ordered the other workers to reject all their stones and throw them far from the tower. But not a single stone near the tower was rejected — they were all placed in the building because they were smooth and shining. **5** Many stones from the large number lying far off were rejected, however. He directed these to be sorted into separate piles — some in one heap, some in another, some in a third. But the twelve mountains were not piled up; they were arranged in order according to their individual appearance. **6** When the stones had been placed in the building, the man called to me: "Come here, Hermas." I went to him and said, "Lord, do you call for me?" He replied, "What would you like to know?" "Lord," I said, "I want to understand the whole vision from beginning to end — the meaning of the placed stones, the rejected ones, those thrown far away, and why the building has not yet been completed."

---

### Council Notes

The great lord who suddenly appears (v. 1) is the most majestic figure in the Shepherd's Visions. He combines three symbolic elements: the crown (kingship), the sickle (judgment/harvest, Revelation 14:14-20), and the shepherd's crook (pastoral care, John 10). Together these identify him as Christ, though the Shepherd never states this explicitly.

His being "taller than the tower" is significant: the figure of Christ transcends the Church he governs.

The sorting of rejected stones into "separate piles" (v. 5) suggests a taxonomy of the rejected — not all rejection is equal. The twelve mountains are arranged separately, maintaining their individual character even in rejection.

Hermas's final question (v. 6) drives the remainder of Vision 3: why is the building not yet finished? The answer will involve the theology of repentance.
